opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, moving between the two has been one of the most formative things in my career, because each world forces you to ask different questions.

In academia, at Caltech, the questions are about foundations. Why does this work? What are the guarantees? Can we build methods that generalize beyond the narrow benchmark we tested on? That's where a lot of my early work on tensor methods came from: wanting algorithms with provable properties rather than just empirical tricks.

Industry, first at Amazon and then at NVIDIA, gave me a very different perspective. There you see scale up close: the compute, the data, the engineering needed to make something actually run on thousands of GPUs. And you see real users with real problems that don't fit neatly into an academic framing. That pushed me to think about where the bottlenecks really are, not where they're theoretically interesting.

What I've come to appreciate is that the most impactful work lives right at that intersection. Neural operators are a good example. The mathematical idea of learning mappings between function spaces came from a very principled place, but it only became useful for weather forecasting, climate modeling, or fluid dynamics because we could scale it on modern hardware and work with domain scientists who had concrete needs. Something like FourCastNet doesn't happen with theory alone or engineering alone.

So my approach now is to keep that loop tight: start from principled foundations, test them against real-world scale and messiness, and let what breaks feed back into the theory. And I try to bring that mindset to my students too, so they're not just chasing leaderboard numbers but also not stuck in purely abstract settings that never touch reality.

r001.rationale: She says her work is most impactful at the intersection of principled mathematical foundations and industry-scale engineering, and describes using real-world constraints to inform theory.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that each side keeps the other side honest.

In academia, at Caltech, I get to ask questions where the payoff might be a decade out. Things like neural operators, where we're learning solution operators for partial differential equations instead of training a model on a fixed grid. Nobody in a product org is going to fund that in year one, because there's no obvious revenue line. But that's exactly the kind of work that ends up mattering, because it changes what's possible rather than optimizing what already exists.

Then industry, and my years at NVIDIA and at Amazon before that, taught me something academia tends to underweight, which is that scale is not a detail. It's a research question in itself. When you actually try to run a weather model like FourCastNet operationally, or build a foundation model that has to serve real users, you discover that the elegant idea on the whiteboard breaks in ways you could never have predicted from a small benchmark. Data pipelines, numerical stability at scale, the cost of inference. Those constraints shaped my theoretical questions. They told me which problems were real.

So my approach now is to insist on both ends of the pipeline. I want the math to be principled, with guarantees where we can get them, and I want it running on real hardware against real scientific or engineering problems. Tensor methods were like that for me early on. The theory was beautiful, but it only became compelling when it was running on GPUs on actual data.

The other thing industry gave me is a sense of urgency and humility about who the end user is. In academia the audience is often other researchers. In industry the audience is someone trying to design a better aircraft wing, or predict a hurricane path, or model a fusion reactor. That reframing, AI as a tool for scientists and engineers rather than an end in itself, is probably the single biggest influence on how I pick problems today.

And frankly, the reverse flow matters too. Students bring a fearlessness that big organizations lose. Some of the best ideas my group has had came from a student who didn't know a thing was supposed to be impossible. Moving between the two worlds lets me carry that energy into places that need it, and carry the discipline of scale back into the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says academia enables principled, long-term theory while industry teaches the demands of scale and real-world deployment, and describes bringing both into her research.

astra-6.text:
For me, academia and industry have been very complementary. Academia gives you the freedom to step back and ask fundamental questions: Why does a method work? What are its limitations? Can we develop a better mathematical foundation? In industry, you encounter the practical constraints—data, computation, scale—and you see where those assumptions break down.

That creates a feedback loop. Practical challenges motivate new research, and research can open up possibilities beyond improving an existing system. It has shaped my approach to AI as both a scientific discipline and a tool for scientific discovery. I want to understand the underlying principles, but I also want to build methods that are useful outside the settings in which we developed them.

r001.rationale: It describes academia as a place to develop fundamental questions and mathematical foundations, industry as exposing practical constraints, and the feedback loop between research and practical challenges, clearly connecting theory with practice.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, industry and academia offer complementary perspectives. Academia gives me the freedom to ask fundamental questions and explore ideas whose impact may take years to become clear. Industry brings me closer to practical constraints: Can we scale this method? Is it reliable? Does it solve a problem that matters?

Moving between those environments encourages me to connect theory with practice. Practical challenges can expose gaps in our understanding and inspire new research, while fundamental research can open up possibilities we wouldn’t discover through incremental engineering alone. I think that exchange is especially valuable in AI, where progress requires both ambitious ideas and careful execution.

r001.rationale: The response says that moving between industry and academia encourages her to connect theory with practice, and explains how each setting informs the other.
